title: Γεωργὸς καὶ τύχη
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 84 (= Perry 61). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.l: A certain farmer, while digging, came upon gold.
sentences.n: χρυσίον is the diminutive of χρυσός, used of gold as a thing found and handled — a piece or a hoard of it. περιτυγχάνω takes the dative of what one falls in with.

sentences.t: Καθ’ ἑκάστην οὖν τὴν Γῆν, ὡς ὑπ’ αὐτῆς εὐεργετηθείς, ἔστεφε.
sentences.tr: Kath’ hekastēn oun tēn Gēn, hōs hyp’ autēs euergetētheis, estephe.
sentences.l: So day by day he garlanded the Earth, as having been well treated by her.
sentences.i: So every day he crowned Earth with garlands, on the ground that she had done him the kindness.
sentences.n: καθ’ ἑκάστην leaves ἡμέραν unsaid — 'day by day'. ὡς with a participle gives the reason as the agent himself sees it, not as the narrator vouches for it; the whole fable hangs on that distinction. Γῆ with a capital is the goddess, and garlanding a god's image or altar is an ordinary Greek gesture of thanks.

sentences.t: Τῷ δὲ ἡ Τύχη ἐπιστᾶσά φησιν· « Ὦ οὗτος, τί τῇ Γῇ τὰ ἐμὰ δῶρα προσανατίθης, ἅπερ ἐγώ σοι δέδωκα, πλουτίσαι σε βουλομένη ;
sentences.tr: Tōi de hē Tychē epistasa phēsin· « Ō houtos, ti tēi Gēi ta ema dōra prosanatithēs, haper egō soi dedōka, ploutisai se boulomenē ;
sentences.l: But Fortune, having stood over him, says: « You there, why do you dedicate to Earth my gifts, which I have given you, wishing to make you rich?
sentences.i: But Fortune stood over him and said: « You there — why do you make over to Earth gifts of mine, which I have given you myself, meaning to make you rich?
sentences.n: ἐπιστᾶσα, 'having stood over', is the regular verb for a god or a dream appearing at a sleeper's or a worker's side; it says nothing about standing up. φησίν is present where the story is past — the vivid narrative present, which Greek slips into at the moment someone speaks. Ὦ οὗτος is brusque, the hail you give a stranger you are not pleased with. Chambry sets a space before his Greek question mark.

sentences.t: Εἰ γὰρ ὁ καιρὸς μεταβάλοι καὶ πρὸς ἑτέρας χεῖρας τοῦτό σοι τὸ χρυσίον ἔλθοι, οἶδ’ ὅτι τηνικαῦτα ἐμὲ τὴν Τύχην μέμψῃ. »
sentences.tr: Ei gar ho kairos metabaloi kai pros heteras cheiras touto soi to chrysion elthoi, oid’ hoti tēnikauta eme tēn Tychēn mempsēi. »
sentences.l: For if the moment should change and this gold of yours should come into other hands, I know that then it is I, Fortune, whom you will blame. »
sentences.n: The optatives μεταβάλοι and ἔλθοι make the supposition remote — 'should it ever happen'; the conclusion then drops into the plain future μέμψῃ, because about that she has no doubt. καιρός is the moment as it stands, the way things happen to be just now. σοι is a dative of possession leaning on the gold: the gold that is yours — for the moment.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι χρὴ τὸν εὐεργέτην ἐπιγινώσκειν καὶ τούτῳ χάριτας ἀποδιδόναι.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti chrē ton euergetēn epiginōskein kai toutōi charitas apodidonai.
sentences.l: The fable shows that one must recognize one's benefactor and render thanks to him.
sentences.n: ἐπιγινώσκω is to know a thing for what it is, to identify it correctly. The farmer's fault is not ingratitude — he is scrupulously grateful — but gratitude aimed at the wrong power.
